turns.doctor_question: Hi, it’s good to meet you. What brings you in today?
turns.patient_response: Well, I came in because... at work, you know, I manage the retail floor, and when I try to explain the inventory numbers or the weekend schedule to the team, my words just start jumping. I'll be talking about the delivery trucks, and then suddenly it's about Thursdays, and then I'm thinking about the church grill we used last summer, which reminds me of my boss's tone of voice when he's annoyed. Speaking of my boss, he always wears these terrible ties, like the ones from the 90s with the little geometric shapes. I think he gets them at thrift stores, which is fine, I like thrift stores too, found a great lamp at one last week... but anyway, people just look at me like they can't follow what I'm saying. They get this blank stare.

symptom_reasoning.S021: The patient explicitly describes and demonstrates their speech jumping between unrelated topics (trucks, Thursdays, church grill, boss's ties, thrift stores), causing others to be unable to follow their train of thought.

turns.doctor_question: During these times when your thoughts and words jump around, do you also feel unusually high or euphoric?
turns.patient_response: High? No, no, I don't feel high or euphoric or anything like that. I just feel regular, you know, just trying to get my point across to the team. It's just normal work stuff. Like dealing with the new seasonal displays they just sent us. They shipped these massive cardboard cutouts this year, and they're taking up half the stockroom right now. Which actually reminds me, my own garage is looking exactly like that stockroom lately. I've been meaning to clean it out, maybe have a yard sale this weekend. Yard sales are funny, aren't they? People will stand there and haggle over fifty cents for a used coffee mug. I have this one mug I got on a trip to Seattle back in '98, it has a little chip on the handle, but I still use it every single morning. The coffee just tastes better out of it, you know? My sister lives near Seattle, actually, in this little house with a green roof...

symptom_reasoning.S021: The patient's response demonstrates tangentiality and loose associations, jumping from work displays to their garage, yard sales, a coffee mug, and their sister in Seattle without a logical flow.
symptom_reasoning.S033: The patient explicitly denies feeling high or euphoric, stating they just feel 'regular'.

turns.doctor_question: Do you ever hear voices when no one else is there?
turns.patient_response: Voices? No, no, I don't hear anybody talking when they aren't there. Just the regular sounds, you know? Like at work, it's mostly just the store radio. They play the exact same forty songs on a loop every single day. I swear, if I hear that one Phil Collins song again... I actually used to love Phil Collins, though. Saw him live back in, oh, must have been '85? Or '86? We drove my buddy's old Ford Bronco all the way to Chicago for the show. Man, that truck was an absolute beast, drank gas like you wouldn't believe. Gas was so much cheaper back then, too. Now you pull up to the pump and it's like taking out a second mortgage just to get to work. My commute isn't even that bad, maybe twenty minutes, but there's this one traffic light on 4th street that stays red for a solid five minutes. I sit there every morning just staring at the bakery on the corner. They make these blueberry scones...

symptom_reasoning.S020: The patient explicitly denies hearing voices or people talking when they aren't there.

turns.doctor_question: Do you ever feel that people are trying to harm you or plot against you?
turns.patient_response: Plot against me? No, I don't think anyone's out to get me or anything like that. People are mostly just focused on themselves, you know? Like at the store, everyone's just rushing to get their shopping done and get home. Though we did have this one guy last Tuesday who tried to walk right out the front doors with a whole cart full of power drills. The new security sensors went off, and let me tell you, those things are incredibly loud now. Almost gives you a heart attack when they trigger. It actually sounds exactly like the fire alarms at my old college dorm. I lived in this massive brick building, third floor, and they'd run these drills at two in the morning in the dead of winter. We'd all be standing out there in the freezing snow in our pajamas. I had these great flannel pajama pants back then, red and black plaid. You really can't find good quality flannel like that anymore. Everything you buy nowadays just shrinks the second you put it in the dryer. I bought a nice button-down shirt just last month, washed it exactly how the tag said, and now the sleeves don't even reach my wrists...

symptom_reasoning.S019: The patient explicitly denies feeling that anyone is out to get them or plotting against them.
symptom_reasoning.S021: The patient's speech exhibits tangentiality, wandering from the initial question to a shoplifter, fire alarms, pajamas, and shrinking clothes without returning to the point.

turns.doctor_question: When you were a child in school, did teachers often say you were easily distracted or had trouble staying on topic?
turns.patient_response: Distracted in school? I don't really remember them saying that, no. I mean, school was a long time ago. I went to this little elementary school, Lincoln Elementary. The building was so old, it had those huge windows that rattled whenever the wind blew hard. And they had these radiators that would hiss and clank all winter long. It was always either freezing cold or boiling hot in those classrooms. My fourth-grade teacher, Mrs. Gable, she used to keep a fan on her desk even in December. She was a real character, Mrs. Gable. She had this massive collection of porcelain frogs. They were everywhere—on her desk, on the bookshelves, even lining the windowsills. I always wondered where she got them all. You know, my aunt had a collection like that, but hers was thimbles. She had thimbles from all over the world. She went on this big cruise to Alaska once and brought back a thimble with a little moose painted on it. I've always wanted to go to Alaska. I saw a documentary about the salmon run up there, and the bears just standing in the river catching them right out of the water. It's amazing how nature works like that...

symptom_reasoning.S021: The patient's speech demonstrates tangentiality and loose associations, drifting from the topic of school to radiators, a teacher's frog collection, an aunt's thimbles, and bears in Alaska.
symptom_reasoning.S008: The patient explicitly denies remembering teachers saying they were easily distracted in school.

turns.doctor_question: Have there been times when you had much more energy than usual?
turns.patient_response: More energy? No, I wouldn't say so. Just my normal, everyday energy, I guess. Especially lately, because corporate decided to send us all the spring patio furniture early this year. It's still freezing out, and we've got boxes of wicker chairs stacked up to the ceiling in the back room. Wicker is so fragile, too. My grandmother had a whole sunroom full of wicker furniture when I was growing up. It was painted white, and the paint would always chip off if you sat on it wrong. We used to sit out there and drink iced tea in the afternoons. She made the absolute best iced tea, always put a little sprig of fresh mint in it from her garden. She had this massive garden out back, grew tomatoes the size of softballs. You really just can't buy tomatoes like that at the grocery store anymore. They always look perfect and red on the shelf, but you bite into them and they just taste like water. I bought a pack of those hothouse tomatoes last week for a sandwich, and it completely ruined the BLT I was making. The bacon was good, though. Thick cut, applewood smoked. I get it from the butcher down on 4th street, the guy with the big handlebar mustache...

I tried knitting once, back in my twenties. I thought it would be a relaxing hobby, but I could never get the tension right. My stitches were either way too tight or so loose they'd fall right off the needles. Needles are funny things, aren't they? They make those bamboo ones now, which seem nice, but I had the metal ones. They clacked together so loudly. It sounded exactly like my neighbor's wind chimes. He has these huge metal pipes hanging on his front porch, and whenever there's a storm, it's just this constant clanging noise. Last week, we had a storm that knocked out the power for three whole blocks. I had to use a flashlight to find my way around the kitchen.
